tables.title: Table 1: Population Size Estimates among Women Engaged in Commercial Sex Using 3-Source Capture Recapture by survey site in Uganda, 2021 - 2023
context: Executive Summary

This report provides findings from a biobehavioral surveys (BBS) among women engaged in commercial sex (WCS), implemented from 2021 - 2023 by the Crane Survey Project, a collaborative activity of Makerere University School of Public Health (MakSPH), Ministry of Health (MoH), the US Agency for International Development (USAID) and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), with funding from the U.S. President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR). The BBS included 12 sites: Arua, Busia, Buvuma, Fort Portal, Gulu, Jinja, Kampala, Lira, Mbale, Mbarara, Masaka and Tororo.

The aim of the BBS was to inform HIV programming and policy in Uganda by estimating prevalence of HIV, syphilis, and Human papillomavirus (HPV), HIV service uptake (ART coverage, viral load suppression, and CD4 cell count) and HIV prevention services such as Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP) and post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP), risky behaviors (alcohol use, drug use), depression, and violence against children. The population size of WCS was estimated and the survey employed Respondent-Driven Sampling (RDS) design. Main survey findings are summarized in Tables 1-3 below.

A total of approximately 3,249 participants were enrolled in the biobehavioral survey across 12 survey sites in Uganda between 2021 and 2023, using respondent-driven sampling. The largest sample was enrolled in Kampala (n≈1,692), followed by Jinja (n≈923) and Arua (n≈634), with the remaining participants distributed across Busia, Buvuma, Gulu, Mbale, Tororo, Mbarara, Masaka, Lira, and Fort Portal. The study population included women engaged in commercial sex (WCS). Estimates presented in this report reflect the combined WCS population unless otherwise specified.

context: Seed selection and recruitment process

Initial survey participants (“seeds”) were recruited by the survey team to start enrollment. Seeds were purposively enrolled to reflect a broad array of sociodemographic characteristics (e.g., age, sexual orientation, education, area of residence, marital status, language, religion), HIV status, and affiliation with a HRP organization or HRP service provider. At the time of their enrollment, seeds were oriented to promote a feeling of survey ownership and enthusiasm about the project. Seeds were provided with coupons to distribute to their peers for enrollment. Instructions for peer recruitment using an enrollment process script were provided to seeds and participants. At the beginning of the survey, 2 - 5 seeds were included per site. The details regarding the number of seeds per site are included in section 2.4.

Survey Sites: Crane Survey offices were located in the 12 sites and cities (i.e., Arua, Busia, Buvuma, Fort Portal, Gulu, Jinja, Kampala, Lira, Masaka, Mbale, Mbarara, Tororo) across the country as shown in the map in Figure 1 below.

2.2 Laboratory Testing

Laboratory testing was carried out both on-site and off-site. Nearby accredited/certified regional referral hospital laboratories conducted tests for HPV, CD4 count and provided viral load samples and DBS temporary storage. Central Public Health Laboratories (CPHL) was responsible for viral load testing and longer DBS storage. Testing using DBS was done at international laboratories at CDC in Atlanta, USA. Material Transfer Agreements (MTA) were signed to enable sample shipment outside Uganda.
2.2.1 Laboratory Procedures

Participants who were eligible and consented had 10 ml of venous blood drawn into EDTA-containing vacutainer tubes. Blood was stored at room temperature or kept at 2-8°C at nearby peripheral hub and later transported to the CPHL where specimens were tested for HIV and CD4+ T cell counts. Samples (plasma) were prepared and transported for storage at CPHL at -20°C and -80 °C with consent of participants to allow future testing. Sample storage conditions in Entebbe met standard conditions, including daily monitoring of temperature.

tables.title: Table 6: Input Parameters and Target Sample Sizes for WCS BBS surveys, Uganda, 2021-2023
context: Target Sample Size estimation

For surveys with an HIV prevalence of >10%, the target sample size aimed to estimate VLS with a precision of no more than +/- 10 percentage points. Assuming a design effect of 2 in RDS surveys (Salganik et al., 2006, Salganik et al., 2010), this meant that to collect VL results for about 200 participants (see Table 7 below for varying scenarios). Our total target sample size therefore varied between 500 and 1,700 (larger HIV prevalence required smaller sample sizes). Further we monitored convergence and bottleneck graphs for VLS and HIV prevalence (See Annex 6) and would continue sampling (and introduce new seeds) if convergence had not been reached for both indicators or severe bottlenecks are observed
To accommodate still circulating (valid) RDS coupons after coupon issuance had been stopped, the final sample sizes slightly exceeded the needed sample sizes or the maximum sample size stated here.

2.4 Seeds and Enrolment

Seeds were participants who initiated in each referral chain and were purposely selected by the investigators in collaboration with the CBOs. Seed selection prioritized individuals with large social networks, positive community standing, and alignment with survey objectives. To ensure independence and diversity, seeds were chosen from various backgrounds based on age, place of residence, education, socioeconomic status. Seeds met the respective eligibility criteria and were given coupons and instructions for peer recruitment.

Seeds and subsequent participants received 3 coupons at the beginning of the survey and as time progressed, the number of coupons given to recruits per survey site depended on the proportion of coupons redeemed to facilitate continued waves and to enable attainment of the desired sampling size. Due to the varying local contexts of these survey sites that is, the social economic, cultural diversities of these environments, enrolment and participation in some areas required bigger or greater number of seeds to try and capture higher, diverse respondents or create new waves of participants to obtain the sample size and also sustain the survey. tables.title: Table 8: Population Size Estimate using three source capture-recapture (3S-CRC) of WCS Surveyed in 12 sites, Uganda, 2021-2023
context: Across the 12 survey sites, a total adjusted sample size of approximately 3,249 WCS participants was achieved. Site-specific enrollment varied, with Kampala contributing the largest proportion of participants (n≈1,692), followed by Jinja (n≈923) and Arua (n≈634). Enrollment at other sites ranged from smaller to moderate sample sizes, reflecting differences in survey duration, recruitment dynamics, and population size across locations. The survey included both adult women engaged in commercial sex (WECS). Although SEM were enrolled and included in relevant analyses, overall enrollment figures were not disaggregated by WECS and SEM, and results are therefore presented for the combined population unless explicitly stated.
3.1 Population Size Estimates using 3-Source Capture Recapture and Demographic Characteristics among WCS Surveyed in 12 Sites, Uganda, 2021-2023

Between 2021 and 2023, the 3SCRC study estimated the population size of WECS across 12 Ugandan cities using both absolute and network-size (SS-PSE) methods. Kampala had the largest estimated number with ~5,000 women (95% CI 3,729-9,941). This represented less than 1% of its female population aged 15-49. The highest relative proportions were found in Gulu (4.5%) and Fort Portal (4.4%), while the lowest were observed in Mbale (1.0%) and Lira (1.0%). Successive sampling estimates were generally lower but showed similar geographic patterns, with relative proportions ranging from 0.8% in Kampala to 3.7% in Lira. Overall, results highlight substantial variation in the size and concentration of female sex worker populations across Ugandan cities, with the highest proportions occurring in smaller urban centers.

Using the three-source capture recapture method, we estimated the number of WCS/ SEM across 12 sites and found that the Kampala had the highest estimated number of WCS followed by Gulu and Tororo. Additional details are included in the table below.
